title: Idomeneo
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 73rd Idomeneo. The very first, in 1982, opened this same Ponnelle production.
Your host, Eric Owens, isn’t just hosting: he’s also the offstage Voice of Neptune in Act III.
James Levine led the Met’s first Idomeneo in 1982 and leads today’s, No. 73. His Met total: 2,577 performances.
The overture’s soft final chords were a setup: they lead straight into G minor, the key of Ilia’s scene.
Recitative comes two ways here: “secco”, with just harpsichord and cello, and orchestral “accompagnato”, which Mozart handles masterfully.
Nadine Sierra, our Ilia, was 28 at this matinee. 2017 was also her Richard Tucker Award year.
Mozart wrote Idamante for a castrato. Alice Coote, known for trouser roles, also sang him in San Francisco in 2008.
Elettra, jealous of Ilia: “I can feel you all in my heart, furies of the dark hell.”
Shipwreck! Mozart builds this scene almost exactly like the storm scene in Gluck’s Iphigénie en Tauride.
Matthew Polenzani made his Met debut in 1997, in Boris Godunov, and has since sung over 300 performances here.
Ponnelle filmed La Cenerentola with Frederica von Stade in 1981. A year later she was his first Met Idamante.
Mozart was 24 when he wrote Idomeneo, his third opera seria, for the Munich court carnival.
Ponnelle’s frame: classical Roman columns, a broad flight of steps, and shifting backdrops of Piranesi-style ruins.
Arbace today: British baritone Alan Opie, who shared Grammys for recordings of Peter Grimes and Die Meistersinger.
Four solo winds join Ilia: flute, oboe, horn, bassoon. Her first singer, Dorothea Wendling, was a flautist’s wife.
Mozart to his father Leopold, Munich, 8 Nov 1780, planning this aria “in concert with four wind instruments”
Mozart wrote this role for Anton Raaff, a 66-year-old star who had sung with Farinelli. It was his last.
For her 2012 Met debut as Queen Elizabeth I, Elza van den Heever shaved her head for the HD close-ups.
Munich’s 1781 review raved about the port and Neptune’s temple scenery, and never mentioned Mozart by name.
Munich press notice of the premiere, 1781
Bon voyage from Sidon, the Cretan port they’re sailing from. Small detail: it’s a fictional city.
Hear the piccolo? It plays only in this storm. A 1982 critic called these perhaps opera’s first realistic tempests.
Critic: F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, reviewing the Met premiere of this Ponnelle staging, Oct 14, 1982
^Introduction\ to\ Act\ III\ by\ Eric\ Owens$
Before he sang, Eric Owens played oboe, taking lessons from Laura Ahlbeck, an oboist in the Met Orchestra.
“Zeffiretti lusinghieri” means “Zephyrs caressing”: alone in the garden, Ilia asks the breezes to carry her love to Idamante.
Mozart on this quartet: “there is no single thing in my opera with which I am so pleased.”
Mozart to his father Leopold, Munich, 27 Dec 1780
Mozart added this march so the king can enter with his whole suite. Scored simply, to be played mezza voce.
Mozart to his father Leopold, Munich, 3 Jan 1781
Mozart’s plan for Neptune: three trombones (heard only here) and two horns, placed with the voice. The orchestra falls silent.
Mozart to his father Leopold, Munich, 3 Jan 1781
At this staging’s 1982 Met premiere, Hildegard Behrens “literally stopped the show” with this aria, ending in collapse.
F. Warren O’Reilly, Washington Times, reviewing the Met premiere of this Ponnelle staging, Oct 14, 1982
Home to D major, the overture’s key. Mozart first closed an opera this way here, then in every one after.
